t.3.60.1: Dejected, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa in a dejected voice: “Lakṣmaṇa, go quickly to the river Godāvarī and find out whether Sītā has gone to the Godāvarī to bring back lotuses.”
t.3.60.2: Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, swift of step, went once again to the lovely river Godāvarī.
t.3.60.3: Having searched that river with its many bathing places, Lakṣmaṇa said to Rāma: "I do not see her at any of the fords, and though I call out, she does not hear me."
t.3.60.4: To what region, then, has she gone, Vaidehī, the dispeller of sorrow? For truly I do not know, O Rāma, the place where she, the slender-waisted one, now is.
t.3.60.5: Having heard the words of Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma, wretched and bewildered by anguish, himself went up to the river Godāvarī.
t.3.60.6: Having come up to it, Rāma spoke thus: "Where is Sītā?"
t.3.60.7: Though she had been carried off by the lord of the rākṣasas, who deserved to be slain, the creatures did not tell Rāma of her, and neither did the river Godāvarī.
t.3.60.9: But the river, recalling that form of Rāvaṇa and the deeds of that evil-souled one, out of fear did not tell him of Vaidehī.
t.3.60.8: Then, though urged by the creatures, saying, "Tell him of his beloved," and though questioned by Rāma, she, herself stricken with sorrow, did not speak of Sītā.
t.3.60.10: Made hopeless of seeing Sītā by that river, Rāma, worn down by not seeing Sītā, spoke to Saumitri.
t.3.60.12: Vaidehī, who dispelled all my sorrow when I, deprived of my kingdom, was living in the forest on forest fare, where indeed has she gone?
t.3.60.11: O Lakṣmaṇa, what unwelcome words shall I speak when I meet Janaka, and the mother as well, coming back without her, without Vaidehī?
t.3.60.14: The Godāvarī, Janasthāna, and this mountain Prasravaṇa, all of these I shall roam through, if indeed Sītā may be seen.
t.3.60.13: Bereft of the support of my kinsmen and not seeing the princess, I think the nights will be long for me as I lie awake.
t.3.60.15: As the two brothers were thus speaking with one another, they saw a trail of flowers fallen upon the earth.
t.3.60.16: Seeing that shower of flowers fallen upon the surface of the earth, the heroic Rāma, grief-stricken, spoke sorrowful words to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.60.17: Lakṣmaṇa, I recognize these flowers here. They are the very ones I gave in the forest, which were worn by Vaidehī.
t.3.60.18: Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, bull among men, the mighty-armed one, enraged, then addressed the mountain there, as a lion addresses a lesser beast.
t.3.60.19: O mountain, show me Sītā, golden of complexion and radiant as gold, before I destroy all your peaks.
t.3.60.20: Scorched by the fire of my arrows, you will be reduced to ashes, stripped of grass, trees and tender shoots, and shunned by all forever.
t.3.60.21: Or else, Lakṣmaṇa, I shall dry up this river today, if she does not tell me now of Sītā, whose face is like the moon.
t.3.60.22: Thus enraged, Rāma, as if wishing to burn everything with his gaze, saw on the ground the huge footprint of the rākṣasa, leading away.
t.3.60.23: Having observed the trampled ground left by Sītā and the rākṣasa, Rāma, his heart agitated, spoke to his dear brother.
t.3.60.24: Look, Lakṣmaṇa, at the golden beads from Vaidehī's ornaments scattered here, O Saumitri, and at her garlands of many kinds as well.
t.3.60.25: Look, Saumitri, the surface of the earth is covered on every side with bright drops of blood that gleam like drops of molten gold.
t.3.60.26: I think, Lakṣmaṇa, that Vaidehī, torn apart again and again by rākṣasas who take any form at will, will have been divided among them or devoured.
t.3.60.28: And whose is this great bow, studded with pearls and gems and adorned with refined gold, lying broken and fallen upon the ground, O gentle one?
t.3.60.27: With Vaidehī as its cause, O Saumitri, a terrible battle took place here between two rākṣasas who were quarrelling over her.
t.3.60.29: Whose is this golden coat of mail, shining like the young rising sun and studded with beads of beryl, lying shattered upon the ground?
t.3.60.30: And whose is this parasol with a hundred ribs, adorned with heavenly garlands, its staff broken, cast down upon the ground, O gentle one?
t.3.60.31: And these fierce ones with golden breastplates and Piśāca faces, terrible in form and huge of body: whose are they, lying slain in battle?
t.3.60.32: Whose war chariot is this, gleaming like a blazing fire, radiant, bearing its battle standard, now flung aside and broken?
t.3.60.33: These arrows, as long as chariot axles and adorned with refined gold, lie broken and scattered here. Whose are they, this one of terrible deeds?
t.3.60.34: Behold, gentle one, this hundredfold enmity of mine, which will end my life, with the rākṣasas of most dreadful hearts, who change their forms at will.
t.3.60.35: Sītā has surely been carried off, or she is dead, or the poor woman has been devoured; dharma does not protect Sītā as she is being carried away in the great forest.
t.3.60.36: For if Vaidehī has been devoured, or even carried off, O Lakṣmaṇa, which lords in the world, gentle one, are able to do what is dear to me?
t.3.60.38: Surely the lords of the thirty gods think me powerless, because I am gentle, devoted to the welfare of the world, self-controlled and compassionate.
t.3.60.37: O Lakṣmaṇa, out of ignorance all beings would hold in contempt even the maker of the worlds, a hero, if he is known for his compassion.
t.3.60.39: See, Lakṣmaṇa: having come to me, virtue has turned into a fault. This very day, for the destruction of all beings and of the rākṣasas, I am like the great sun that has risen after withdrawing the moonlight.
t.3.60.40: Neither Yakṣas nor Gandharvas, neither Piśācas nor Rākṣasas, nor Kiṃnaras nor humans shall find any happiness, O Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.60.41: Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, the sky filled with my missiles and arrows! Today I shall make it impassable for those who move through the three worlds.
t.3.60.42: You will see a world whose hosts of planets are held back and whose moon is veiled, shrouded over, with fire, wind and the radiance of the sun all vanished.
t.3.60.43: the world with its mountain peaks shattered, its lakes drying up, its trees, creepers and shrubs destroyed, and its oceans laid waste.
t.3.60.44: If the lords do not give that Sītā back to me safe and well, then in this very moment, O Saumitri, they shall see my might.
t.3.60.45: O Lakṣmaṇa, no creature will fly up into the sky, for it will be filled without a gap by the nets of arrows loosed from the strings of my bow.
t.3.60.47: For the sake of Maithilī, with arrows drawn back to the ear and hard to ward off, I shall make the world of the living free of piśācas and free of rākṣasas.
t.3.60.46: Behold today, Lakṣmaṇa, the world tormented by my iron arrows, its beasts and birds slain or fleeing in confusion, thrown into utter turmoil and stripped of all its bounds.
t.3.60.48: Today the gods shall see the might of my arrows, driven by my wrath, loosed in my fury, and flying to great distances.
t.3.60.49: Neither gods nor Daiteyas, neither Piśācas nor Rākṣasas will remain when the three worlds have been utterly destroyed by my wrath.
t.3.60.50: The worlds of the Devas, Dānavas and Yakṣas, and those of the Rākṣasas as well, shattered to pieces by floods of arrows, shall fall apart in many ways. Today with my arrows I shall make these worlds bereft of all bounds.
t.3.60.51: Just as old age, as death, as time, and as fate are never warded off among all beings, O Lakṣmaṇa, so I too, filled with wrath, cannot be held back, without a doubt.
t.3.60.52: If they do not show me today, as before, Sītā the Maithilī, blameless and lovely-toothed, I will overturn the whole world with its gods, Gandharvas, men and serpents, together with its mountains.
